title: User Experience (UX) Design
section: 12. Web Design School - Create a Website that People Love
summary: UX is the invisible quality of a site that lets people do what they want without effort. Covers five UX principles (simplicity, consistency, reading patterns, all-platform design, testing) and a tour of dark patterns to avoid.

concepts.heading: UX versus visual design
points: Visual design imposes an aesthetic; good UX is nearly invisible because everything just feels easy.
A campus-path story illustrates the idea: wait to see where people actually walk, then pave those routes. Design around observed behaviour, not assumptions.

concepts.heading: 1. Simplicity
points: Prefer the simpler option whenever you choose between simple and complex.

Contrast: a very dense news portal packed with links overwhelms the reader, while a magazine-style news site breaks content into varied chunks (text, images, video, quotes) with a consistent colour scheme and typography.

concepts.heading: 2. Consistency
points: Keep both look and behaviour consistent across the site. Example: a telecom company's pages each had a differently styled navigation bar with moved buttons and a relocating search box, forcing users to relearn the site on each section.
Inconsistency hurts most for less technical or older users.

concepts.heading: 3. Reading patterns
points: F-pattern: the eye scans across the top, then a shorter scan lower down, then moves down the left edge. Put key content, bullets, icons and buttons along the left, with the logo at top-left. Suited to text-heavy pages.
Z-pattern: the eye zigzags from top-left to top-right, diagonally down, then across the bottom. Suited to sparser pages with more media or fast browsing; a social network landing page is the example.
Place content where people naturally look.

concepts.heading: 4. All-platform design
points: Sites must work on phones and desktops: mobile responsive layouts that rearrange rather than just shrinking.
A desktop layout squeezed onto a phone gives tiny links that are hard to tap. The reverse also fails: a narrow mobile-style layout on a wide monitor leaves vast unused space.
Avoid stacking so many banners, cookie notices and warnings on mobile that the actual content area is tiny. Equally, do not scale a single image or text block to fill an enormous scroll.
(Extra) In CSS this is done with the viewport meta tag, media queries, flexible units and max-width containers.

concepts.heading: 5. Test with real people
points: Get feedback from professional testers if possible, otherwise friends and family. Observe what confuses them and iterate.

concepts.heading: Dark patterns
points: Dark patterns use design psychology to push users toward actions that benefit the company rather than the user. They count as bad UX.
Misleading hierarchy: highlighting the paid express delivery button in a bright colour so people click it instead of the free option they wanted.
Disguised ads: a one-pixel line in a mobile ad that looks like a hair on the screen so that swiping at it registers as a click.
Hidden opt-outs: an airline checkout where the 'no travel insurance' choice is buried in a long alphabetical country-style dropdown rather than shown as an obvious option.
Confusing double-negative checkbox wording so users cannot tell what ticking the box will do.
Good design helps people do what they want to do; the packaging analogy is a sandwich that looks full-size but is mostly air.

concepts.heading: Lead-in to the project
points: The next lecture applies colour, typography, UI and UX to designing a hotel website from scratch.

pitfalls: Cramming dense link lists or content onto one page.
Navigation that changes style or behaviour between sections.
Designing only for desktop, or only for mobile.
Using dark patterns such as hidden opt-outs and misleading button emphasis.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'UX basics': blurb on simplicity, consistency and responsiveness. Tasks: 1) make navigation identical on two pages; 2) simplify a cluttered page; 3) add a viewport meta tag and a media query so cards stack on mobile; 4) lay out a landing page along the F or Z pattern; 5) rewrite a dark-pattern checkout so the opt-out is obvious.
Starter code idea: a two-page site with inconsistent navbars and a fixed-width desktop-only layout.
Interactive demo idea: toggle between desktop and phone widths on the same page, with an F/Z-pattern overlay and a dark-pattern spotting quiz.
